# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Gets Upstairs

Water is heavy, lazy, and stubborn. It doesn't want to climb thirty stories, and it certainly doesn't want to do so on demand at 6 a.m. when ten thousand showers turn on simultaneously. The fact that it does anyway is a quiet triumph of engineering, and understanding it requires only a few physical principles applied with remarkable consistency.

## The Fundamental Problem: Elevation

Start with the physics. Water pressure in a static column is determined entirely by elevation. Every 2.31 feet of vertical rise costs you one pound per square inch (psi) of pressure. This is the single most important number in water distribution. A reservoir sitting at a certain elevation provides "hydraulic head"—the energy stored in the water simply by being high up—and that head is what pushes water through pipes to your tap.

Consider a concrete example. Imagine a city with a reservoir impounded behind a dam in hills to the north, with the water surface at 620 feet above sea level. The downtown district sits at 140 feet.
